An inconvenient experiment in interpreting data beyond visual conformity.

Daily Rate of LIVE BIRTHS and DEATHS

How Jorge Camões’s conventional cycle plot disrupted my dataviz instincts

I recently came across a cycle-plot visualization designed by Jorge Camões, a data visualization expert for whom I have developed tremendous respect over the years. Because that respect has been mutual, I have always felt free to follow and comment on his work without being constrained by the usual social-media formalities.

The visualization was posted on LinkedIn with the following note:

“Love #cycleplots. Often used for data with strong seasonality, but I wanted to compare these two variables, live births and deaths, check if I could spot some patterns at month level. The results are... depressing.”

It is hard to fault Jorge when it comes to dataviz choices. Once in a while, I feel like showing another perspective, but this was not really one of those cases. What triggered me was the content of the visualization itself: a chart meant to reveal similarities across 12 panels, yet similarities my eye could not easily extract. And because I value data smoothing, both for noise removal and pattern detection, we quickly exchanged a few comments. At some point, however, I felt the subject had exactly the kind of substance I like to approach through a carefully crafted numerical framework. The goal was not to replace a beautifully made visualization, but to expose the structure behind it through the right methodology, in a way that supports and strengthens the kind of cognition cycle plots invite.

This project is a numerical journey and reasoning I want to share.

The first thing that comes into play with cycle plots is the cycle itself: seasonality. But to see seasonality properly, the data first has to be stripped of noise. My first quick check was therefore to look at the data from its trend perspective over the years, and then redisplay that trend in the same cycle-plot structure.

That immediately triggered Jorge’s reaction: there was no obvious monthly pattern variation. And he was right. By using only the trend, I could only reveal the general time variation, which was then almost identically inherited by each month. For a moment I found myself defending the numerical mechanism, but there was actually nothing to defend. The trend extraction was not wrong. It was simply not enough for this investigation. By isolating the trend, I had unintentionally hidden the seasonal component, exactly the component that made the cycle plot interesting in the first place.

So I moved to a seasonal-trend decomposition and I posted the following reply. That immediately raised the real questions: should I look at the trend, the seasonality, or their reconstructed combination? Should the raw data remain visible? Could births, deaths, and balance be shown together without clutter? Could they share a compatible scale? And, more importantly, was a simple additive decomposition really adequate, especially given the irregularity visible in the colder months?

A standard STL approach decomposes the series into trend, seasonality, and residuals, usually through LOESS smoothing and an additive logic: Signal = Trend + Seasonality + Residual. Next to that, it also exists a multiplicative logic: Signal = Trend × Seasonality × Residual, for which we can use the same method, using a cyclic logarithmic-exponential-logarithmic transformation. I tried both of them, and the results were almost indistinguishable. But that was not the real issue. The real issue was methodological: how could I avoid manually deciding whether the data should be treated as additive or multiplicative?

That led me back to the decomposition mechanism itself. I replaced LOESS with Whittaker smoothing, a century-old method that remains one of the most elegant smoothers available. Its great advantage here is that smoothness can be selected through cross-validation, making the result less dependent on personal visual preference and more directly related to the data.

The second step was to avoid choosing manually between additive and multiplicative behavior. For that I used a Box-Cox transformation, again selected by cross-validation. In this setting, the Box-Cox power controls where the decomposition sits between additive-like and multiplicative-like behavior. The selected power is not decorative; it changes the transformed space in which trend and seasonality are extracted.

At that point, the method became more than a response to one chart. It became a reusable decomposition and encoding framework. Once it worked for Portugal, I extended it to all suitable geo entities with at least a decade of complete data.

Once the data was extracted, I was facing a genuinely multidimensional problem. Cycle plots are generous on their own, but the split into twelve monthly spaces made it harder than I expected to follow both the independent monthly trajectories and the relationships between them. In 2D, the usual choice is brutal: either overlap and create clutter, or separate and make comparison harder.

That was the moment when 3D became an option to me. Thing is that the seasonal extraction was already, internally, a surface smoother. The surface existed as a numerical mechanism, hidden from the viewer. Showing that surface directly became probably the most intuitive visual moment of the whole project.

A short step back in time may explain why this felt natural to me. By origin, I am a mechanical engineer. A few centuries ago, when I started working as an engineer, technical drawings were the main way information moved between designer and fabricator. Front views, top views, side views, sectional views: all of them were disciplined ways of slicing a three-dimensional object into readable two-dimensional projections. Those rules of sectioning and displaying technical information still hold today, and they will continue to hold. Then, in the mid-1990s, with the rapid rise of CAD systems, a new direction became dominant: 3D modeling. Despite its early difficulties, adoption was universal. Today, rarely is a technical drawing sent to production without its corresponding 3D model.

This is exactly where my mind went with the data. After more than 15 years in the data visualization community, I have acknowledged, praised, and often defended the accuracy and conventions of 2D encoding. I have also contributed my own numerically grounded representations. Yet one question kept bothering me: how many of our conventions exist because the flat surface forces us to choose one projection, one section, one compromise?

In my view, we have reached a wall of 2D representability. For the sake of decoding accuracy on flat surfaces, we have deliberately kept depth and motion outside the serious vocabulary of data visualization. We keep circling around the precision of 2D encodings, which is understandable, but also limiting.

I am not expecting a Great Schism in data visualization. It may remain a small cult with one member. Still, I decided to give it a shot and build projects that work in four dimensions rather than two: horizontal position, vertical position, depth, and motion. Yes, this requires interactive media. But we already live inside interactive media almost every day. We do not simply read screens anymore. We touch them, rotate them, zoom them, drag them, search through them, and expect them to respond.

So why should graphical decoding remain locked inside the habits of paper? Why not extend our perceptual vocabulary by using two additional dimensions at once, when the medium already allows it?

Of course, this cannot be done by throwing raw data into 3D and hoping the result becomes meaningful. The data has to be transformed into a readable signal. It has to be aggregated, decomposed, or shaped into a perspective that can actually be understood in 3D and explored through motion. This is not about journalism or storytelling in the usual sense. It is about numerical investigation and exploration reflected through visualization.

Obviously, the twelve cycle plots feel a lot like technical sections. Useful, readable, and familiar, but still sections. The decomposition model had already produced a continuous seasonal-trend surface. Displaying it as a virtual 3D object was the natural next step.

Once I was able to encode the 3D information, I've added some show/hide controls and I was starting to experiment visualization that can be read beyond impressive achievmeent of graphical technology. Raw data became just a reference, trend, trend + seasonality, trend+seasonality + residuals representated as thorns, instead of classic inter-area design. yearly and monthly sections became a a dynamic investigation, rotating view on different perspectives reveal both trends, seasonalities, exceptions. alternative wires direction shown not only the signal but also the bydirectional relationship between dimensions. Time and cyclic evolution. Stopping into the section or projection we need to measure using our trained mind in 2D.

Obviously I dont plan to throw away 2D, it was never my intention. Just like in the technical drawings nowadays. They still hold the same strong 2D representation and annotation conventions. But a 4D model can be our next level addon. One that can build ad hoc 2D perspectives we crafted all along ourselves.

Daily Rate over Years

Use the top-right button to customize the view. Activate Cyclic wires from the menu and lower the surface opacity for a visual exploratory orthographic projection. In this view, the wires behave like a standard spaghetti chart, making the monhly trajectories easier to compare. For a better visibility combine with 3D exploration.

Daily Rate over Months

Similarily, activate Annual wires from the menu and lower the surface opacity for the counterpart annual spaghetti chart. Show or hide the surface of interest.

Daily Rates Heatmap over Years and Months

Increase surface opacity to reveal the intersection, either between the births and deaths surfaces or between the balance surface and the zero plane. For each month, this intersection marks the year when daily death rates overtake daily birth rates, or vice versa. Wires are not useful in this view; when activated, they read more like gridlines.
